In the time that I have been covering Xinjiang, which has been quite a while, the tone of discourse about China in the United States has changed a lot. When I started covering Xinjiang, the current iteration of policies in Xinjiang, which started around 2016–2017, this was the issue that all of the foreign journalists in China were always talking about. It was like this thing where you couldn't get readers to pay attention. It was like a fringe issue about this group of people, the Uyghurs, who nobody knew existed.

Since then it has become a huge issue. Several governments, including the United States, have labeled the policy as genocide. It has attracted international sanctions and contributed to the U.S. diplomatic boycott of the Olympics. There are certain things that I think all reporters can do better on China. One is, for instance, not using the construction "the Chinese." There are word choices and things at the line level you can do better. I try to do all of those things, but I try to frame my reporting and my role in a really narrow way.

Remidio : Journey so far
Remidio's journey was sparked by a fortuitous encounter with an ophthalmologist during a train journey in 2009. It dawned on us that while the cost of treating eye diseases had come down, the cost of testing for an eye disease remained prohibitive. Moreover, 60% of a specialist doctor’s time was spent not on treatment but rather finding out if a patient had a problem. This, we believed, was not an efficient utilisation of an ophthalmologist’s time. We then asked ourselves: Can we decentralise eye testing, especially for vision-threatening chronic eye diseases?

Our initial focus at Remidio was on creating user-friendly retinal imaging devices that could reach even the remotest corners, whether in India or a developed nation like the United States. However, when we began delivering these devices for chronic retinal disease screening, we noticed that individuals sought assistance, not just for retinal issues but for any form of visual impairment, in these decentralised contexts. This prompted us to delve into the realm of comprehensive eye screening. We aimed to address all potential diseases that, if detected early, could avert unnecessary blindness.

Our efforts extended beyond the retina, evolving around 2016–2017, as we successfully addressed the challenge of taking multiple portable devices to remote areas. Nevertheless, the absence of doctors in these areas meant we had to rely on teleophthalmology and infrastructure to triage patients to specialist clinics. This prompted us to explore the development of ‘on the edge’ AI solutions at this critical juncture that are designed to work within the constraints of a developing nation context.

Remidio’s journey with their AI solutions
In contrast to the prevailing approach adopted by many global AI giants, we recognised that in India, we needed a solution that could do instant triaging that didn't rely on infrastructure like the internet, electricity, or cloud-based inferencing—things not easy to find in the last mile.

The period spanning from 2018 to around 2020–21 was dedicated to developing our own technology—what we refer to as "on the edge," "on-premise," or "on-device" AI—that is clinically sensitive but able to run on low-processor environments like a smartphone.

From 2020 to 2023, we embarked on a journey to seamlessly integrate AI and devices.

We must frankly admit that some things are hidden from our eyes. We really do not understand, for instance, the relationships between time and eternity, nor do we have much of an idea how the God who inhabits eternity discloses himself to us in our finite, space/time history. It is revealed that he does; we have various words to describe certain elements of this disclosure (e.g. incarnation, accommodation). But we do not know how. Yet in none of these cases is this a subtle appeal to ignorance, or an irresponsible hiding behind the irrational or the mystical. When we admit—indeed, insist—that there are mysteries about these matters, we do not admit that they are nonsensical or self-contradictory. Rather, we are saying that we do not know enough, and we admit our ignorance. What God has not disclosed of himself we cannot know. The secret things belong to God.

Indeed, because of the contrast in the text, the implication is that it would be presumptuous to claim we do know, or even to spend too much time trying to find out—lest we should be presuming on God's exclusive terrain. Evers has emphasized the need to expand paid family leave, a proposal that was turned down by the Legislature in the previous year. He urged Republicans to take action on this issue. Additionally, Evers called for increased investment in mental health services across the state.
